---
title: "Data management"
subtitle: "How study data is organised, delivered, and joined"
---

This page describes the conventions you need to know to work with **NCC-study
(Koronastudien)** data: how datasets are structured, what the different
delivery formats are, how sensitive data is separated, and how to join data
sources correctly. It is aimed at researchers and analysts using the delivered
data — not at the people maintaining the processing pipeline.

::: {.callout-important}
## All NCC data lives on TSD

Study data is highly sensitive and never leaves **TSD** (Tjenester for
Sensitive Data). You analyse it inside TSD; you bring *results* out by hand,
never person-level data. Nothing on this public documentation site contains
real data, participant identifiers, or internal server paths — and neither
should anything you copy out of TSD. See
[Reproducible analysis](reproducible-analysis.qmd) for the "code in / results
out" workflow.
:::

## The shape of the data

Every delivered dataset — whether a single questionnaire file, a topic-specific
dataset, or the full legacy dataset — follows the same three rules. Together
these make any two files safe to join.

1. **`deltaker_id` is the join key.** It is the unique participant identifier
   and appears as the first column of every file. It is the *only* key you ever
   join on.
2. **One row per participant.** Delivered datasets are in **wide** format: one
   row per `deltaker_id`, no duplicates. Longitudinal registry data is
   pre-summarised to wide before delivery, so it never causes fan-out.
3. **Variable names are globally unique.** Every variable is prefixed with its
   form, so columns from different files never collide when joined.

::: {.callout-tip}
Because of rules 1–3, joining is always a clean `1:1` merge on `deltaker_id`.
If a join produces more rows than participants, something is wrong — stop and
check before analysing.
:::

### Variable prefixes

Each questionnaire item is prefixed with the form it came from. Derived and
computed variables have their own prefixes.

| Prefix | Meaning | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `B_`   | Baseline (B1, B2) | `B_Age_gr` |
| `F1_`–`F6_` | Follow-up questionnaires | `F6_Hospitalised_v2` |
| `R1_`–`R6_` | CLOC sub-study reports | `R3_Report_date` |
| `E1_`–`E3_` | Extra questionnaires | `E2_RAND12_gh` |
| `Q1_`  | Quick questionnaire | `Q1_Symptoms` |
| `deriv_` | Derived cross-form variable | `deriv_infection_status` |
| `gen_` | Computed scale score | `gen_phq9_sum` |
| `C1_`  | Composite / combined variable | `C1_vaccine_status` |

Knowing the prefix tells you at a glance which source a variable came from and
which file you need in order to have it.

## Labelled data

Delivered files are **labelled**: variables carry a human-readable variable
label and, for categorical items, value labels. Both Norwegian and English
labels are maintained. In R these arrive as `haven_labelled` vectors.

::: {.callout-note}
Treat labels as documentation, not as data. Convert to explicit factors when
you need the text (e.g. `haven::as_factor()`), and keep the underlying codes
for modelling. Never hard-code a label string as a filter condition — value
*codes* are stable across releases, label wording may be refined.
:::

Question text and value labels are the semantic definition of an item and are
stable even when the underlying variable name changes between pipeline
versions. If you are ever unsure what a variable means, the label — not the
name — is the source of truth. A **codebook** (variable names, labels, value
labels, types) is delivered alongside every dataset.

## Which dataset should I use?

Two delivery modes are produced from the same underlying per-form files, so
they are always mutually consistent.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Topic datasets (recommended for new work)

Curated, pre-assembled datasets scoped to a research area — e.g. CLOC, long
COVID, vaccine. Each contains only the forms, registry data, and derived
variables relevant to that topic. They are **smaller, faster to load, and
easier to reason about**. Start here for any new project.

```
cloc_dataset.qs
long_covid_dataset.qs
vaccine_dataset.qs
```

### Legacy full dataset

A single wide dataset joining all forms with all derived variables, mirroring
the historical `full_deriv.qs`. Variable names, prefixes, and derived variables
match the old pipeline, so **existing analysis scripts keep working
unchanged**. It is large and memory-hungry — use it only when you specifically
need backward compatibility with an established pipeline.

```
full_deriv.qs
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb
New project → topic dataset. Maintaining an old pipeline that already loads
`full_deriv.qs` → keep using the legacy dataset until you have time to migrate.
Both are built from the same source data, so results agree.
:::

## Data sensitivity: research vs admin tiers

Data is separated into two tiers by sensitivity. As a researcher you work in
the **research (yellow)** tier.

| Tier | Access | Contains |
|------|--------|----------|
| **Research (yellow)** | Researchers + admins | Delivered per-form files, topic and legacy datasets, codebooks. Free-text / elaboration fields are **suppressed**. |
| **Admin (black/red)** | Data managers only | Full files including free-text elaboration fields and raw consent data. |

Free-text and open-ended "elaboration" fields (typically named `*_elaborate`),
and any field that could re-identify a participant, are classified as sensitive
and are **not** present in the research-tier files.

### Requesting sensitive fields

If your analysis genuinely needs a suppressed field — for example free-text
responses for a qualitative analysis — the data manager can assemble a custom
dataset that includes *only* the specific sensitive columns you need, alongside
your standard research variables. This custom dataset is shared with you
individually and does not enter the general research area.

::: {.callout-note}
Every release of admin-tier data is an explicit, logged action by the data
manager — it is not something you can trigger yourself. Request it early if you
anticipate needing it.
:::

## Joining datasets

All joins are `1:1` on `deltaker_id`. Pick the join type by which participants
you want to keep.

| Goal | Join | Result |
|------|------|--------|
| Everyone from both files | **full join** | Keeps all participants; `NA` for forms not completed |
| Only those who completed both | **inner join** | Smaller; no cross-form missingness |
| Start from one file, enrich it | **left join** | Keeps all rows of the left file |

For most cohort analyses, **full join** is the safe default: it preserves the
whole cohort and represents non-participation as missing rather than silently
dropping people.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```r
library(dplyr)
library(qs)          # or qs2 for newer files

b1 <- qread(here::here("B1.qs"))
f1 <- qread(here::here("F1.qs"))
f2 <- qread(here::here("F2.qs"))

# Full join — keep the whole cohort
df <- b1 |>
  full_join(f1, by = "deltaker_id") |>
  full_join(f2, by = "deltaker_id")

# Sanity check: no join should increase the participant count
stopifnot(nrow(df) == n_distinct(df$deltaker_id))
```

### Stata

```stata
use "B1.dta", clear

merge 1:1 deltaker_id using "F1.dta", nogenerate
merge 1:1 deltaker_id using "F2.dta", nogenerate

* _merge == 1  only in base (did not complete the other form)
* _merge == 2  only in using file
* _merge == 3  in both
```

### SPSS

```spss
* Sort every file by the key before matching.
GET FILE='B1.sav'.
SORT CASES BY deltaker_id.
SAVE OUTFILE='B1_sorted.sav'.

GET FILE='F1.sav'.
SORT CASES BY deltaker_id.
SAVE OUTFILE='F1_sorted.sav'.

MATCH FILES
  /FILE='B1_sorted.sav'
  /FILE='F1_sorted.sav'
  /BY deltaker_id.
EXECUTE.
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Always verify the row count after joining. A `1:1` merge on `deltaker_id`
should never produce more rows than there are participants. If it does, you
have likely picked up a file that is not deduplicated — do not proceed.
:::

## Good practice checklist

- [ ] Start from a **topic dataset** unless you specifically need legacy
  compatibility.
- [ ] Join **only** on `deltaker_id`, and check the row count afterwards.
- [ ] Read variable meanings from the **label / codebook**, not the name.
- [ ] Filter on value **codes**, not label text.
- [ ] Request any **sensitive fields** from the data manager early.
- [ ] Keep all person-level data inside **TSD** — export results only.
